opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that most unlearning methods are post hoc. You train a model on everything, and the knowledge you want removed ends up deeply entangled with everything else the model knows. Then you come in afterward and try to surgically suppress it, usually by fine-tuning with some objective like gradient ascent on the forget set, or by steering the representations away from certain outputs.

What we keep seeing is that these methods mostly change the model's *behavior* rather than its underlying *knowledge*. The information is still sitting there in the weights; it's just been made harder to elicit. So if you do a little bit of fine-tuning afterward, even on seemingly unrelated or benign data, or you use a cleverly worded prompt, or you probe the internal representations, the supposedly forgotten information comes right back. It's more like obfuscation than true forgetting.

And there's a fundamental tension there. Knowledge in these models isn't stored in neat, isolated compartments. Facts about, say, a hazardous topic share representations with a lot of general, useful knowledge. So if you push hard enough to really erase the target information, you start damaging the model's general capabilities. If you're gentle enough to preserve utility, you typically only get that shallow, superficial suppression. Existing methods tend to land on the shallow side of that trade-off.

So part of what we've been thinking about is whether you need to intervene earlier, during pretraining itself, and shape *where* and *how* certain knowledge gets stored, so that removing it later is actually feasible, rather than trying to undo an entangled mess after the fact.

r001.rationale: It describes gradient ascent on the forget set and says pushing for true erasure can damage the model’s general capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says knowledge is not stored in neat, isolated compartments and that facts share representations with useful knowledge.

r003.rationale: It identifies entangled, poorly separated knowledge as a reason post hoc unlearning tends to suppress behavior without truly removing information.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core issue is that most of these unlearning methods are operating on the wrong object. They're trying to get the model to stop producing a particular output, and they measure success by whether that output disappears. But the knowledge isn't stored as an output. It's distributed across the representations, and what you've really done in most cases is teach the model to suppress the behavior in the contexts you tested.

So you end up with something that looks like forgetting but is really more like a thin layer of refusal or redirection sitting on top of intact knowledge. And the evidence for that is how fragile it is. You fine-tune on a small amount of unrelated data, or you rephrase the query, or you do a little bit of adversarial prompting, and the information comes right back. If the model had actually forgotten, that wouldn't happen. Relearning something from scratch should take real effort, and instead it's nearly free, which tells you the underlying representations were never touched.

The second thing I'd point to is the evaluation problem. The benchmarks we've had for unlearning mostly check whether the model answers a fixed set of questions about the forget set. That's a very narrow probe, and it's exactly the kind of thing gradient-based methods are good at gaming. If you optimize against a loss that says "don't say this," you'll find the cheapest path to not saying it, and the cheapest path is almost never deep removal. So the methods and the metrics have been co-evolving in a way that rewards shallow solutions.

And then there's a more fundamental tension. Knowledge in these models is entangled. The facts you want to remove share parameters and representations with general capabilities you want to keep. If you push hard enough to actually disrupt the target knowledge, you start damaging everything around it. So the methods that preserve utility tend to be the ones that do the least real unlearning, and the ones that do more unlearning tend to break the model. Nobody has really found a way to get both, and I'm not sure the current paradigm of post-hoc gradient updates is where that answer lives.

What I think is more promising is reframing the question. Instead of asking "how do I remove this after the fact," ask what it would take for the model to be robust to relearning, or whether you can structure training so that certain information is localized enough to be removable. Those are harder questions, but they're at least pointed at the actual problem rather than at the symptom.

r001.rationale: The response says that stronger attempts to disrupt target knowledge can damage surrounding capabilities, but it does not explain this specifically as fine-tuning to produce high loss on the targeted information.

r002.rationale: The response describes knowledge as entangled across shared parameters and representations, but does not state that training gives no reason to expect it to be disentangled into selectively erasable neurons or subspaces.

r003.rationale: The response identifies entangled knowledge and poor separation as a reason unlearning struggles: facts share parameters and representations, so removing target knowledge risks damaging nearby capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the challenge is that we don’t have a very clear way to distinguish between a model forgetting something and a model learning not to say it. A lot of methods can make the model stop producing a particular answer when you ask directly. But that doesn’t necessarily mean the underlying information is gone. If you change the prompt or give it a little additional context, that information might still be accessible.

And information isn’t stored in a language model as a collection of independent records that you can just delete. The same parameters support many different capabilities, and a fact might be learned from many different examples. So you’re trying to remove something very specific without damaging everything else the model knows. That’s a difficult problem both for designing the methods and for evaluating whether they’ve actually worked.

r001.rationale: It says removing a specific fact risks damaging other things the model knows, but does not explain that fine-tuning for high loss on targeted information can cause that damage.

r002.rationale: It says model parameters support many capabilities and facts may come from many examples, but does not state that training gives no reason to expect information to be disentangled into selectively erasable neurons or subspaces.

r003.rationale: It identifies information as not being stored in independent, easily removable records and explains that shared parameters and overlapping examples make selective removal difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the challenge is that we don’t have a very clear definition of what it means for a model to forget something. If you ask it a question and it no longer gives you the answer, did it actually forget, or did we just change how it responds to that particular prompt? The information might still be accessible if you ask differently, or it might come back with a little bit of fine-tuning.

And information isn’t necessarily stored in one isolated place that we can go in and erase. It’s tied up with other things the model has learned. So there’s this tension between removing the information you care about and preserving the capabilities you want to keep. Existing methods can look successful under a particular test, but that’s a much weaker requirement than reliably removing the information across all the ways someone might try to recover it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions that fine-tuning might recover information, but does not say that training for high loss on targeted information can destroy other information.

r002.rationale: It says information is tied up with other things, but does not state that training gives no reason to expect information to be separated into selectively erasable neurons or subspaces.

r003.rationale: The response says information is tied up with other learned material, creating a tension between removing it and preserving capabilities, and presents this as a challenge for reliable unlearning.
